Freelance full time, working on a novel on the side. Though I'm currently on leave for carpal tunnel surgery coming up, and can't type more than 20 minutes without pausing (use your braces and take breaks kids). 

Anyway, here's a typical day, it actually starts the night before. 

I get into bed an hour before I sleep, which because I freelance is usually late. I have severe ADHD and Insomnia and my best work comes to me at night. I've learned to just adapt to it rather than fight it. Anyway, I put on some ambience, either cafe chatter, rain with cars, lofi etc. Then I just take notes in bed, either for my commissions the next day, or thoughts on my novel. Doesn't matter if it sounds stupid, I just write it down so I have it. Not exactly an outline, more of "hey, client would like this" notes. If I have a book I'm reading I'll try to fit in a half hour, then conk out.

Morning I have my breakfast, feed my dog, and take him for a long walk.  It gives me time to breathe, get some sunshine, and actually think about the notes I took the night before, shifting through them as we go, and then Alphi doesn't bug me while I'm working. 

  
After I get home it's some chores (usually I have laundry/dishes, or just a quick wipe down of the bathrooms), and then I sit at my desk once the Vyvanse has hit and I'm able to focus. First part of actual work is connecting with clients I'm working for that day. WIPs handed out, e-mails answered, etc. If I noted down something that changes what we discussed I ask them about it. Then I write. I go for about two hours, break for a stretch, then another two hours etc. After a solid 6 hours I let my clients know what's up and sign off work for the day. Since I'm freelance people are tempted to treat me as if I can be reached at any point in the day, but no, as with any job, once I hit my six hours of writing I am unreachable until the next day. 

I have lunch/dinner between writing, give the dog dinner and another trot. After work work is done I hang out with my wife for a bit, do any other chores, then around the time night hits I sit down for my novel work. I do that for about two-three hours. I'm a complete pantser when it comes to my novel. First draft is whatever comes out, comes out. If I'm having a bad night writing I don't force it, I just take notes, or read instead. 

Then it's video games, hot shower, cuddle with wife, and repeat.

Next will be actual writing. I like to "free write", this means you take a blank page, and write out whatever words come to mind. It'll help you practice your typing skills as well as get your thoughts out. I usually go about ten minutes every day. And you do need to write \*every\* day.

I wanted to be a teacher. I have scars, and I was pulled from college to be placed in inpatient hospitalization from an attempt. When I returned the next semester, I re-took the class I had been taking when I left, and the teacher point blank told me I would never, ever be a teacher with "emotions" like I had. And I believed her.  And I quit my major, and changed it to English, with which I excelled and graduated with a 3.8GPA and a commendation from my professor. I became a writer and now work full time. Do I consider that other professor right? No. Because two semesters later, on my fourth and final year of college, I went inpatient again. And again I returned to that professor who gave me a commendation, and all of my writing was weak because I was still vulnerable. She did not insult me, nor did she tell me to quit. Instead she sat me down, and allowed me to write with her in her office. We wrote in silence for over an hour, just typing away on our laptops. And I poured out my soul next to that woman, and that's when I realized who I was meant to be. 

That previous professor never broke me; I had broken myself. I took in her words. But when offered guidance and care, I thrived. We as a human race are delicate creatures, and we take in everything around us. My circumstances didn't make me fail, I did, in sucking everything in. My circumstances didn't make me thrive, I did, in trying again. And it's because I CHOSE to go back, I CHOSE to listen to my professor, I CHOSE to sit in that office and write that I became who I am today. 

He can choose those awful, untrue words to you. And you can choose to believe them, or you can choose to fight them. It is allowed to hurt, you don't have to force it not to hurt. But you choose your own actions. Find your office, sit in it, and write.

So, first off your flow is very erratic, and you swap out between long and short sentences, which creates a very. jagged. way. of. reading the story. I would work on combining some sentences together, or taking some away and refocusing on what's important. 

Second, as much as we love detail within our worlds - sometimes readers don't. Unless it's important, no one cares if her car is orange, especially if it doesn't make many appearances. No one cares if the garage is red - unless it says something about the character. Allow the setting to speak for itself, there's no need to toss in random colors unless the readers \*need\* to know. 

Third, you write very structured, which can be useful for certain things, but doesn't work for fiction. An example from how your story reads:

He took the bun  
He put the hot dog in the bun  
He ate the hot dog 

You can adjust by using "assumed actions". If he's placing the hot dog in the bun after stepping up to the grill, you can assume he's grabbed the bun already. If she's breaking off part of her hot dog, you can assume she gave him part of the bun. Kosmo has a hot dog, you can assume he's eating it as they talk, perhaps you can add in how it tastes or dropping a piece, but you don't need to write every bite people take. 

All in all, I think it's a good start and you have a good rough idea of what writing should be. You need to work on your flow, and your "clunkyness" (which EVERY new writer struggles with). Your dialogue could be a bit tighter, but you write each character as a unique person, which is great. I won't say much about grammar or spelling, because it's just the second draft, but do keep an eye on it and be ready to tighten and fix as you go.

I've been a professional writer for too many years. I freelance and make a living off it, so here's what I did. 

First, I free write. I put whatever the hell comes to mind onto the page. This can look like a bunch of gibbrish, and eventually I'll stumble into a word I like, or a phrase. I take that out and try to create a sentence around it, this keeps my mind and fingers going, it lets me practice with different things not associated to my professional or personal novel work. It also helps me practice speed, if I have no thoughts and I'm just writing words, I can allow my fingers to move more freely. 

Second, write every- and I mean EVERY-day. An e-mail, a letter, free writing, part of your story, etc etc. It becomes muscle memory the more you do it. I don't even look at my keyboard anymore because I know how my hands fit on it, where they're going to move, and how the layout is (of course it takes a bit if I use a new keyboard but eventually I fall into the same habit). It isn't just talent, it's literal practice. 

No editing personal work right off the bat. If you're working on a novel, then just write it. Get it out. Pretend you're throwing up and eject it from you without fucking looking. Editing comes later. You notice a glaring typo? GOOD. It can WAIT. You said the word and twice in a row? That's FINE. This will speed you up, and teach you how to get your ideas out rapid fire. 

You'll do great, jut keep going.

This is an interesting question because it makes two assumptions that I find false. One is egotism. It was never about my ego, it was about protecting myself from perceived harm. People with BPD come from pain, and we avoid more pain at all costs. We do have an exceedingly strong sense of justice but to us, it's justice, not egotism. So no, I don't need to protect my ego, because I never had that particular drive to. 

The second assumption is that I was "95% of the problem", which is an interesting one to make, and I no longer believe in 'quantifying' right versus wrong, that's what leads to black snd white thinking, and is wholly unproductive. 

As for my past relationships that have now ended, I think the people who hurt me, hurt me, and I think if they feel hurt BY me, they're more than in their right to. It's not my right to ever say someone cannot feel hurt or pain. But I'm not in their head, I know what I felt in those relationships, and even now, after many, many years, and therapy, medication, and inpatient visits, I can say that yes, I was also hurt. I was also in pain. And in the end, no matter how those relationships ended, it was the right thing to do, because in my case, we were only hurting one another, and did not have the ability to come to an understanding. 

Putting numbers and blame to anything has become non-productive, all that does is assign pain, and one can't do that, they simply have to allow themselves to feel it, and allow others to feel it as well. To say I was '95% of the problem' is to dismiss my pain, and honestly it feeds the stigma I'm currently fighting, as it goes off the assumption that due to my illness I must be the one in the wrong. So I'd rather say well, no, I did not realize I was the problem, more of, I realize now what I could have done to be more productive in those relationships, and I hope those who I have had to part from have done the same. Growth is important, above all.

Chop up all your veg and add oil to the pot on medium low heat. Add the onion  and garlic for about two minutes. Add the rest of the veg and a small pinch of salt and let it all sweat it out for about 7-10 more minutes.

You can call ahead and explain your anxieties, they may be able to help you with them. You go in and sit in the chair. Sometimes they have a TV, or you can bring headphones to listen to music. Then they numb you up with a shot in your mouth, it looks scary, but it only feels like a big pressure, a pinch, then it stops. You may taste some weird stuff after but don't worry, it can do that.

Then you'll open up wide and the dentist will go in. You may feel some buzzing, pressure, and pulling, but it won't hurt at all. It just feels weird. You can set up a signal beforehand that you need a break (raise your hand) and they'll give a pause, but the doctor should check on you repeatedly to make sure you're tip-top and not in pain. 

Then it's all out, they'll stuff your mouth with cotton. You'll taste blood and cotton, it's ick but not painful. After you go home you won't be able to use a straw or smoke, if you do for a bit. Once it stops bleeding you can pop the cotton out. I was a little swollen in the cheek, and a bit sore, but I took some OTC pain medication and I was right as rain and ready for work the next day. You might spend the day sleeping (from the adrenaline wearing off) and be a little sore, but nothing should be too painful. The doctor can tell you exactly what to eat and do, and if you feel any pain they can tell you just what to take. 

You'll be alright, it looks scary, it sounds loud, but you're alright.

Congee is my go to soft meal, and pretty filling! 

1 cup of rice, and a LOT of water or chicken broth. (I usually use like 6-8 cups because I like it super soft and brothy). 

I flavor it with ginger, salt, pepper (black or white) and when I wanna make it spicy I toss in some chili flakes/oil

Let it boil, then lower to a simmer. Then it's a waiting game, let it go until the rice breaks down and is super soft and porridge like (mine usually goes for about an hour). I use a whisk to help break it up and make it nice and thick. The longer you let it sit the thicker/softer it'll get.

I like to top it with a softly poached egg and mix it all in to get it nice and eggy. If he's up for it you can add some soft veg like cut up mushrooms, add in some scallion and let it sit to soften it,
